territorial_scope.description: Reaches any person or business that makes an AI companion platform available to a user in the Commonwealth, with no stated location requirement for the operator.

evidence.quote: A person or business that makes an AI companion platform available to a user in this Commonwealth.

summary.short: Pennsylvania bill requiring operators of AI companion platforms to disclose AI status, maintain suicide and self-harm safeguards, and add minor protections (reminders every three hours, sexual-content measures, notice of unsuitability), enforced by the Attorney General with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation; takes effect in 120 days.
summary.long: The bill, introduced in the Pennsylvania General Assembly, regulates operators of AI companion platforms made available to users in the Commonwealth. An AI companion is defined as an AI system designed to simulate a sustained human or human-like relationship through retained personal information, unprompted emotion-based questions or ongoing personal dialogue, with listed exclusions for customer-service, productivity, research, video-game bots and certain speaker devices. Operators must issue a clear and conspicuous notice that the companion is artificially generated and not human where a reasonable person would be misled (Sec. 3(a)). They must maintain and implement, to the extent technologically feasible, a protocol to prevent suicidal ideation, suicide or self-harm content and content directly encouraging violence, including crisis referrals, and publish its details online (Sec. 3(b)). For users the operator knows or should have known are minors, operators must disclose AI interaction, give default break-and-reminder notices at least every three hours, and institute reasonable measures against sexually explicit visual material; where a service is offered to known minors, operators must disclose on the platform that AI companions may not be suitable for some minors (Sec. 3(c)-(d)). Section 4 excludes the underlying AI model unless it is directly offered, configured or deployed as an AI companion. The Attorney General enforces the act; an operator that violates it is liable, in addition to other remedies, for a civil penalty not to exceed $10,000 per violation, collected in a civil action (Sec. 5). The act takes effect in 120 days (Sec. 6). The text contains no private right of action.

relations.note: Section 2 defines 'sexually explicit conduct' by reference to 18 U.S.C. § 2256; the term is used in Sections 3(c)(3) and 3(c)(3)'s prohibition on instructing a minor. The target is a federal statute outside the registry.

evidence.quote: As defined in 18 U.S.C. § 2256 (relating to definitions for chapter).

notes: The text contains no legal basis, amendment, repeal or transposition clauses; the only relation is the definitional cross-reference. Capitalized passages in Sections 3(c), 3(d) and 5(b) ('OR SHOULD HAVE KNOWN', 'IF A SERVICE IS OFFERED...', 'AN operator', 'IN ADDITION TO ANY OTHER REMEDY PROVIDED BY LAW') are not marked as inserted or deleted text in the document, so whether they are new matter is not stated in the text. Section 3(c) uses a knew-or-should-have-known standard for minors while Section 3(d) uses 'knows'. Section 6 sets the effective date as '120 days' without stating an anchor event. Document is the bill as introduced; no later version is provided.

thresholds.variable_text: Minor: an individual in this Commonwealth under 18 years of age
thresholds.measurement: Individual's age; the text does not specify how age is determined or verified.
thresholds.consequence: An individual in the Commonwealth under 18 is a minor for this act, which brings the minor safeguards in Section 3(c) and the disclosure in Section 3(d) into play.
thresholds.conditions: The individual must be in the Commonwealth. The safeguards in Section 3(c) apply only where the operator knows or should have known the user is a minor.
